addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

The interaction pattern — Qwen (saturated, pos_sim > 0.98) shows smaller gap than StarCoder (healthy, pos_sim ~ 0.80) — suggests representation geometry mediates strategy effectiveness. neg_difficulty margin analysis (+17% Qwen, +28% StarCoder) provides mechanistic evidence for this interaction. Pending: multi-seed confirmation + plan_005 stratified analysis + plan_015 dynamic mining control. This is reported as an observation with mechanistic hypothesis, not an established finding.\\n\\n3. **Scope-bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis via CodeQL provides a practical pipeline for computing structural connectivity at scale.** 0% timeout, 78% connected-not-gold rate (Z%), 123/131 repos with output at full scale. Frame as practical tool that enables the study, not a standalone contribution.]\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n\\n- **Problem**: Repo-level code repair requires selecting relevant files from large codebases. Current retrievers rely on text similarity alone, but lexical similarity ≠ structural relevance. Hard negative mining is the standard approach to improve contrastive retrievers, yet the field lacks systematic understanding of what negative selection strategies work for code and why.\\n\\n- **Existing approaches & gaps**:\\n  - Text-based retrieval (SweRank, SWE-Fixer): blind to structural dependencies\\n  - Graph-guided at inference (LocAgent, RANGER, CodexGraph): structural graphs at inference only, no training signal\\n  - ARISE: data-flow but intra-procedural only (no call boundary crossing), runtime tool calls only\\n  - CoCoHaNeRe (ACM TOSEM 2025): argues gradient-based hard negative methods outperform non-differentiable embedding negatives — but does not test simple static embedding-distance mining in structural code retrieval settings\\n  - Gap: no systematic study comparing negative mining strategies with proper controls, and no mechanistic explanation for when/why each strategy works\\n\\n- **Our contribution**: A systematic analysis of hard negative mining strategies for contrastive code retrieval. When the pretrained space is saturated (high pos_sim → low margin between positive and negative), the encoder needs harder negatives from an orthogonal signal dimension (structure). When the space has healthy separation, embedding-distance mining alone captures sufficient difficulty gradient. This encoder-strategy interaction, if confirmed, could help explain contradictory findings in prior work.\\n\\n## Dual-Pillar Motivation\\n\\n1. **Primary — Systematic analysis challenging gradient-based assumptions**: Prior work (CoCoHaNeRe, ACM TOSEM 2025) assumes expensive gradient-based hard negative methods are necessary for effective code search. Our controlled comparison shows simple static embedding-distance mining suffices in structural code retrieval, isolating the effect of each strategy.\\n2. **Secondary — Mechanistic explanation via representation geometry**: neg_difficulty analysis (margin distribution × strategy × encoder) provides explanatory depth beyond empirical comparison, offering a candidate heuristic (pos_sim threshold) that, if validated on more encoders, could help practitioners select strategies without exhaustive experiments.\\n\\n## Formal Definition\\n\\nGiven retrieval domain D, structural graph G, similarity function s, query q:\\n**structure-grounded hard negative** = argmax_{x ∈ D : s(x,q) > τ ∧ ¬reachable_G(x,q)} s(x,q)\\n\\nThe structural graph is externally fixed and does not update with the encoder (drift-immune).\\n\\n## Title Options\\n\\n- Primary: \\\"What Makes Hard Negatives Work for Code Retrieval? Contribution is understanding, not just a new method.\\n2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.\\n3. **Against \\\"incremental\\\" criticism**: Paper challenges a prevalent assumption + provides mechanistic explanation for strategy × encoder interaction + validates on downstream task. 2. **NLP audience**: Frame as contrastive learning methodology with code as instantiation. Representation geometry analysis generalizes beyond code.
3. **Against "incremental" criticism**: Paper challenges a prevalent assumption + provides mechanistic explanation for strategy × encoder interaction + validates on downstream task. Three contributions, not one marginal improvement.

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

| Concern | Response | Evidence |
|---------|----------|----------|
| Only 2 encoders — can you generalize? | n=2 is minimum for interaction claim; we frame as observation with mechanism, not universal law; two decoder-only encoders with distinct pretraining (Fill vs FIM) and representation geometry (pos_sim 0.99 vs 0.80) provide meaningful variation | plan_013 (done), m2_full runs |
| BM25 vs true embedding negatives? | Run BM25 negatives to empirically compare with embedding-distance mining, grounding the comparison against CoCoHaNeRe's gradient-based premise | plan_018 |
| Pool size sensitivity? | Evaluate at pool {50, 100, 200, 500} to confirm strategy rankings hold at realistic sizes | plan_019 |
| Stratified by structural data availability? | Report per-stratum R@1 for 34% with structural data vs 66% fallback | plan_005 (extended) |
| Temperature regime specificity | Ablate τ ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} | plan_014 |
| No downstream task evaluation | SWE-bench Lite end-to-end with LLM agent | plan_003 |
| Static vs dynamic mining confound | Clarify mining is static; add dynamic baseline | plan_015 |
| CodeQL scalability at larger scale | 0% timeout, 78% Z%, 123 repos; m1_reextract_v2 adds more | plan_006 (done) |
| Why not compare inference-time graph methods? | Complementary: they navigate at inference, we mine at training. Discuss relationship. | plan_017 |
| Single benchmark | Add RepoBench-R cross-file retrieval | plan_004 |
| Statistical significance | Bootstrap 95% CI for all comparisons; full M2 = 9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders | plan_016, m2_full |
| "Complementary signal" overstatement | Temper: "conditionally beneficial" not "always complementary" | Writing discipline |
| Missing related work | RepoFusion, GRACE, GraphCodeBERT, ANCE, curriculum HN mining | Writing task |

## Evidence Status

### Confirmed findings (basis for claims):
- D017: True embedding mining helps (+2.0pp Qwen, +1.6pp StarCoder) — challenges gradient-based necessity assumption
- D021/neg_difficulty: Qwen pos_sim=0.9855 (saturated), StarCoder pos_sim=0.7985 (healthy); margin differential explains strategy interaction
- m2_embed_verify (pilot): 3-strategy comparison confirms ranking (embedding > random, dataflow conditional)
- plan_013 (StarCoder pilot): Confirms cross-encoder pattern — embedding helps both, dataflow helps Qwen only
- plan_006: CodeQL scalability confirmed at 123-repo scale

### In progress:
- m2_full_qwen: random s42 DONE (R@1=0.5527), s43 DONE (R@1=0.5554), s44 RUNNING (eval@500 R@1=0.6009). 2/10 runs complete, ~50h remaining.
- m2_full_starcoder: random s42 DONE (R@1=0.4604, from parent), s43 RUNNING (eval@500 R@1=0.4708). 1/9+ runs complete, ~65-70h remaining.
- m1_reextract_v2: 80.8% complete (22,842/28,276), 0 ERROR, ETA ~15:00 CST May 15

### Planned (priority order):
- plan_018: BM25 negative baseline (Dream #1 consensus gap — grounds comparison against CoCoHaNeRe's premise)
- plan_003: SWE-bench Lite eval (biggest lever for paper strength)
- plan_019: Pool size sensitivity (Dream consensus — external validity)
- plan_014: Temperature ablation (Dream reviewer concern)
- plan_004: RepoBench-R second benchmark (with multi-seed CIs)
- plan_015: Dynamic mining baseline
- plan_005: Stratified analysis (extended: structural-available vs fallback stratum)
- plan_007/008/009: Additional ablations

## Contingency (if full M2 results weaken claims)

### All 18 runs confirm pilot pattern: Best case
- Full statistical power, paper as framed above
- Target: EMNLP Main

### Dataflow benefit disappears even for Qwen at full scale: Pivot to 2-claim paper
- Drop Claim 2 to analysis observation
- Paper becomes: "Simple embedding mining suffices (challenging gradient-based assumption) + CodeQL extraction is practical + representation geometry analysis explains prior contradictions"
- Still publishable: challenging gradient-based assumption + mechanistic analysis is sufficient for EMNLP Main

### BM25 negatives ≈ random (not harmful): Narrative pivot needed [D030 contingency]
- If plan_018 shows BM25 negatives perform ≈ random (not << random), the "challenging gradient-based assumption" narrative needs adjustment
- Pivot: "systematic comparison reveals embedding-distance mining is the only strategy that consistently helps; gradient-based methods may not be necessary even when BM25 provides no signal"
- Paper remains valid as systematic analysis — the core finding (simple embedding mining suffices) stands regardless of BM25 outcome
- Claim 1 core preserved: "Simple static embedding-distance mining consistently improves code retrieval without gradient-based mechanisms"
- Impact: BM25 result determines narrative nuance, not core contribution

### Embedding mining also loses advantage at full scale: Major reassessment needed
- Recheck data pipeline for bugs (full-scale data may have distribution differences)
- If confirmed: negative result paper — "Why Hard Negative Mining Doesn't Scale for Code Retrieval"
- Discuss with user before committing direction

## Deprecated Claims (with reason)

- ~~"Embedding-distance hard negatives actively harm code retrieval"~~ — FALSIFIED by D017. Original evidence (-27pp R@1) was from BM25-proxy negatives incorrectly labeled as embedding_distance in MVP. True embedding mining shows consistent improvement. Preserved here to prevent regression.
